turns.prompt_text: I have this idea for organizing a file system better I think file systems are really nice because they use that hierarchical structure but the one issue I do have with them is that they are confined to that structure. I would like to have more perspectives, more views and really what this means is that every single file, every element, every unit is actually flat across space like in a graph. And then each hierarchy is essentially a view. Where every unit exists across all views or can be brought into all views. Every element must exist in at least one view. Otherwise they are kind of like in the dark web. I guess there could be a way to go and find things that have no views but they essentially would need a garbage collection system. My theory is that by having many views you can have a lot greater organization due to all the different dimensions that are accounted for. I am wondering if there is a better way to do this because I'm sure people have tried this but I don't know why computers aren't structured this way or why Google Drive isn't structured this way. Why have I never seen it?
turns.response_html:
You've essentially hit on the exact philosophy behind modern personal knowledge systems (like Obsidian graph structures or Notion databases) and database-backed file systems, but scaling that concept down to an operating-system level comes with massive trade-offs.

The core reason computers and cloud storage aren't built this way by default isn't a lack of imagination—it's a fundamental war between query flexibility and system performance, determinism, and portability.

The Performance and Scale Wall

  • Tree traversal vs. graph traversal: Traditional hierarchical filesystems are ruthlessly efficient. Locating a file is just walking a single path of pointers ($/home/user/docs/file.txt$). In a pure graph-based filesystem where files exist in floating space and hierarchies are just dynamic views, every directory listing requires running database-like queries or graph traversals to dynamically assemble folders on the fly. At scale, this adds noticeable latency.
  • Metadata overhead: Every file needs an immutable, globally unique identifier (UUID) coupled with a dynamic tagging/relation ledger. While trivial for a few thousand text notes, indexing millions of system binaries, cache fragments, and application dependencies this way introduces heavy database maintenance overhead at the OS kernel level.

Portability and Interoperability Nightmares

  • The "dark web" garbage collection problem: As you noted, files without views need a garbage collector. But what happens when you plug your drive into another computer, or share a file via email, or upload it to a web form? Standard operating systems and protocols don't understand multi-view graph metadata. A file stripped of its database context defaults back to flat storage or loses its organizational dimensions entirely.
  • Application friction: Most software is built around the POSIX file system standard—it expects an absolute file path. If an app tries to write a temp file or save a config, it needs a definitive, unambiguous address. Abstracting paths into dynamic "views" breaks legacy software unless every application is rewritten to query a central graph daemon.

Why Google Drive and OSs Resist This

  • Mental models: Hierarchies are rigid, but they are cognitively cheap. Humans understand "put document in folder" instantly because it mimics physical filing cabinets. Multi-dimensional tagging requires active curation; the moment a user stops maintaining the tags or views, the graph collapses into digital clutter that is actually harder to search than a messy folder tree.
  • The search compromise: Modern operating systems (like macOS Spotlight or Windows Search) and cloud platforms (like Google Drive) solved this exact problem without throwing out the folder tree. They keep the folder structure for deterministic storage and fallback, but layer a virtual graph on top via indexing, metadata tags, and shortcuts. Google Drive lets a single file live in multiple folders using shortcuts precisely because true multi-parenting breaks sync protocols and user mental models.

True tag- and view-based operating systems have been attempted before (like BeOS's BFS metadata fields, WinFS in the Longhorn era, or modern semantic desktop projects), but they always stall out because users ultimately want files to "live" somewhere predictable.

Are you thinking about building a custom prototype or utility to test this out for specific files, or looking for ways to bridge this gap in your current workflow?

turns.prompt_text: I understand how useful hierarchical file systems are. However I often find myself tripping over my own feet. I've been thinking about using tagging systems. Right now I'm essentially using a default hierarchical system that I've just arbitrarily chosen to go with. But then I have to have extra boards to describe the other dimensions: the tags and so and whatnot. I guess it would be okay to have a default, which is a tree structure, but then to have other structures that live on top of it. Because that default is necessary for the scale operating systems to function and for ease of use however for those who want a more advanced control approach, they can use Extra Views.
turns.response_html:
That "two-tier" hybrid architecture—keeping a dead-simple physical hierarchy on disk while layering dynamic, multi-dimensional views on top—is by far the most resilient way to solve this. It gives you the determinism and compatibility of standard POSIX paths without trapping your workflow inside a single mental model.

When implementing this, there are three proven architectural patterns for structuring those "Extra Views" over a static disk tree.

1. Virtual Filesystems via FUSE (The OS-Integrated Approach) Instead of forcing the underlying filesystem to change, you run a user-space daemon (via FUSE) that exposes a virtual mount point.

  • Under the hood: All actual files sit in a flat store or standard /data/storage/ tree, named deterministically by UUID or timestamp. A lightweight local SQLite or embedded key-value database tracks metadata, frontmatter, and tags.
  • The presentation: The FUSE driver translates database queries into virtual directories. Navigating to /views/by-project/client-a/ or /views/by-type/cad/ dynamically queries the index and presents symlinks or virtual file descriptors.
  • Trade-off: Fully native to the OS (any terminal command or file picker works), but requires maintaining a background indexing daemon and handling virtual write operations cleanly.

2. Symlink/Hardlink Projection Graphs (The Low-Overhead Approach) If you want zero runtime overhead and complete offline portability, your views can be materialized directly using link trees.

  • Under the hood: The physical files live in a basic, single-dimension folder tree (e.g., partitioned purely by year/month or asset type).
  • The presentation: A local script or build tool reads an index/manifest file (or parses file frontmatter/tags) and generates directories filled with symlinks representing different perspectives:
    • ~/views/active-sprints/...
    • ~/views/topics/...
  • Trade-off: Instant and robust across standard backup tools, but requires running a sync trigger whenever tags or metadata change to rebuild/prune dead links.

3. Application-Layer Query Engines (The Database-First Approach) Instead of relying on the OS file browser to navigate files, you treat the filesystem as "cold storage" and do all organization through an engine with dynamic queries (similar to Notion database views or Dataview in Obsidian).

  • Under the hood: Files hold their own metadata in headers (YAML/JSON frontmatter, extended file attributes, or sidecar files).
  • The presentation: You interact with your data via dynamic table/board/graph views rendered by a query tool or a dedicated local UI. Files are grouped, filtered, and aggregated on the fly without ever touching their physical on-disk location.
  • Trade-off: Extreme flexibility and expressive multi-property filtering, but navigation is confined to specific applications rather than standard system dialogues.

Key Design Considerations for a Multi-View System

  • Metadata Locality: Decide whether metadata lives inside the file (e.g., frontmatter in text/markdown, EXIF in images, sidecar .meta files for binaries) or in a central database. Sidecars and embedded tags make files self-describing and portable; a central database makes global queries significantly faster.
  • Primary Key vs. Path: The default hierarchy should be trivial and stable—like YYYY/MM/filename or uuid_filename—so files never need to be renamed or physically moved when their conceptual tags change.
  • Write Semantics: Decide if views are strictly read-only query projections or if moving a file into a virtual view folder should automatically apply that view's tags to the file's metadata.

How are you thinking about maintaining the metadata itself—are you leaning toward file-embedded tags/sidecars, or a central index to drive the views?
